newsitem.title: USA: No shortage of heating oil expected this winter.
newsitem.headline: No shortage of heating oil expected this winter.

text.p: U.S. homes should have enough heating oil to warm them this winter, as long as it is milder than last winter, but consumers are likely to pay more for their fuel, the Energy Information Administration said Monday.
The EIA's outlook was positive, despite its warnings earlier this month that winter fuels would be in short supply because stocks were very thin.
"I don't think you have a shortage situation, because a high price will always be able to find product somewhere," said EIA administrator Jay Hakes.
About 12 percent of U.S. homes depend on heating oil. Three quarters of that supply is used in the Northeast.

"As year-over-year distillate demand growth for the winter season is projected to be only 18,000 barrels a day, supplies from the three major sources -- domestic refinery production, net imports, and primary stocks -- should still be able to accommodate winter fuel requirements," the EIA said in its winter fuels outlook.

If the weather is normal, home heating oil prices should be about 9 cents higher than last winter, averaging about $1.02 between October and March, largely because of the low inventories and higher crude prices, it said.
However, Hakes warned that the outlook depended greatly on weather conditions, which were unpredictable.
"If the U.S. and Europe had cold weather at the same time, that would strain supplies a lot," he said at a news conference.
Stocks of distillates, which include heating oil and diesel fuel, would probably be 19 million barrels below last year's levels at 113 million barrels at the beginning of this winter, the EIA said.
But it projected refinery output of distillate would average 3.25 million barrels per day in October through March, up 53,000 barrels per day or two percent from last winter.

Stocks are far below the average for this time of year over the last five years because of the prolonged winter earlier this year, and higher economic growth, which has fuelled trucking demand for diesel.

Aggravating the situation, markets had built in expectations that distillate prices would fall in the future, giving refiners little incentive to pay the costs of storing diesel and heating oil, Hakes said.

"Additional oil from the North Sea and other non-OPEC countries should provide enough oil for this winter's demand, although a colder than normal winter would greatly increase the likelihood of higher prices, given the little room for error in this year's market," the EIA said.
